1:
The word behind "followers" is stronger than the English, and Clarke makes the most of it. It signifies those who personate another, assuming his gait, his mode of speech, his accent and carriage; it is the word from which we get "mimic," and though that term is now commonly used in ridicule, here it is to be taken in the most solemn sense. Children do this by nature, he adds, copying not only what a parent does and says but insensibly the very tempers of his mind. Robertson notes that Paul uses the old word boldly and draws the plain inference — if we are to be like God we must imitate him. Ellicott calls the phrase unique and striking, and takes the connecting "therefore" to fix the imitation on love above every other attribute; he points out that the startling command to be perfect as the Father is perfect is glossed in the parallel Gospel as being merciful as he is merciful, and cites Hooker on the imitation of God as the law of all moral progress in man. In this idea, he says, lies the distinctive principle of a religious morality as such. Wesley puts the same preference more warmly, asking how much more honourable and happy it is to imitate God than Homer or Virgil or Alexander the Great.

Gill enters the necessary limitation before anyone runs too far with the command. We are not to imitate God in his works of infinite wisdom and almighty power, which is impossible, but in acts of righteousness and holiness, and particularly in mercy, goodness and beneficence — in forgiving injuries and in freely relieving the necessities of the saints, which is what the preceding argument had been about. Calvin thinks the chapter division particularly unhappy for just that reason, since it has cut apart parts of a subject very closely joined; and he quotes an ancient saying to fix the standard, that to sue a man who has injured us is human, to forgo revenge is philosophic, but to repay him with benefits is divine. Henry observes that the imitation puts a great honour upon practical religion, and that the phrase "as dear children" carries its own argument, since children resemble their parents both in the features of their faces and in the dispositions of their minds. Barnes reduces the whole to a question a man may put to himself. If every Christian who is angry, unforgiving and unkind would simply ask how God treats him, it would end, he thinks, all the strife and heart-burning that exists in the church.

The two nouns applied to Christ's death are distinguished carefully by three of them. Barnes takes the first for anything presented to God, in Scripture commonly a bloodless thank-offering, and the second for a proper sacrifice, made by killing an animal and burning it upon an altar, the death acknowledging that the sinner deserved to die. Clarke identifies them with the Hebrew rites, the first answering to the meal-offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense by which gratitude for temporal blessings was expressed, the second to the offering in which blood was poured out for atonement — from which he draws the conclusion that our temporal blessings no less than our spiritual ones come to us through Christ. Ellicott is the most exact. Either word alone bears a general sense, but set side by side they must be held distinct, so that Christ made himself an offering in the perfect obedience of his humility and gave himself a sacrifice when he completed that offering in his blood. He calls the verse a complete summary of the doctrine of the atonement, the more striking for being incidental. Robertson adds one negative, invoking Anselm: the offering was made to God on our behalf, and not to the devil.
3:
The third word in the list divides them. Calvin takes it in the plain sense of an immoderate desire of gain, and Ellicott renders it literally as the insatiable desire for more, distinguishing it from uncleanness as a sin against one's neighbour rather than against one's own body and soul. Gill goes the other way: from its company here, he judges it to mean not the vice commonly so called but a greedy and insatiable appetite after the lusts just named. Clarke tries to hold both. The three terms, he suggests, may be species of one thing, covetousness being excessive indulgence in what is lawful when moderate — for as the covetous man never has enough of wealth, so the pleasure-taker never has enough of the gratifications of sense, the appetite growing by what it feeds on. Yet if simple love of gain is meant, he adds, the company it keeps here shows how degrading it is to the soul and how abominable in the eye of God. Ellicott finds the ambiguity itself instructive, since the Tenth Commandment joins the two kinds of coveting, one temper turning either to lust or to avarice — the first, he suspects, chiefly a vice of youth and the second of age.

Barnes turns the company the word keeps into an indictment of his own age. Paul ranks the covetous man with the sensual and the idolater and shuts him out of the kingdom; is that, Barnes asks, the estimate in which the vice is held now? He answers with four reasons why it is not — that it is so common; that it is found among people making pretensions to refinement and even to religion; that it is harder to define than impurity of life; and that the public conscience has been seared to its groveling character. His own definition is severe: a covetous man is one who in the pursuit of gold neglects his soul, and is regardless of justice, truth, charity, faith, prayer, peace, usefulness and conscience. He closes with a prediction rather than a rebuke — that when the covetous man is ranked in public estimation with the most vicious, the conversion of the world will probably not be far off. Robertson makes the same judgement in a line, that the word stands here in bad company and is debasing like sensuality. Henry notes the alternative reading and calls the love of this world spiritual idolatry, since the epicure makes a god of his belly and the covetous man of his money.

The word for jesting gives the most trouble, since in classical Greek it is a virtue. Clarke defines it from its parts as artfully turned discourse — words easily turned to another meaning, chaste in themselves but conveying an obscene sense from their setting — and adds puns and repartee. Ellicott distinguishes two kinds of foul speech here: the coarse and brutal talk of the fool, and the refined versatility that will find occasion for wit in anything however sacred, fearing nothing so much as to be dull; the first is brutal, the second deadly. He notes the word's respectable classical use as a mean between churlishness and obsequiousness, and observes that it always hovered near the condemnation Christian gravity gives it outright. Barnes is careful to say what is not forbidden — courteousness is commanded, cheerfulness cannot be wrong in men who hope for heaven, and quiet good-natured humour of the kind he finds in Cowper and Addison is not sinful; a smile is not a sin, but levity is not harmless either. Wesley calls the quality a half-virtue among the heathen, and appeals to the experience of tender consciences that even this frequently quenches the Spirit. Clarke asks the sharpest question: how shall a man who has been trifling in company go apart to magnify God for the tongue he has abused?
5:
Chrysostom knows exactly which clause his hearers will want softened. There have always been men, he says, who weaken the hands of the people; when we say that whoever calls his brother a fool goes to hell-fire they answer that it is impossible, and when we say the covetous man is an idolater they call the expression hyperbolical — and by such abatements they explain away all the commandments. Barnes refuses the abatement in his own idiom: to worship money is as real idolatry as to worship a block of stone, and if that is so, what an idolatrous world this is, how many idolaters there are in professedly Christian lands, and how many, it is to be feared, in the church itself. Ellicott traces the descent in two stages. First a man rests on some visible blessing of God as the one thing in which and for which he serves him, and so loses God in God's own gifts; then comes the absolute forgetfulness of him, and the inevitable setting up of some other object to fill the vacant throne. Calvin adds the distinction that keeps the charge exact — this is not the idolatry Scripture usually condemns but another kind, in which a man must deny God to put wealth in his place.

The exclusion sounds harsher than the gospel, and Calvin meets the objection directly. Paul does not say that those who have fallen into these sins and recovered from them go unpardoned; he pronounces sentence on the sins themselves. Writing to Corinth in the same terms he had added at once that such were some of you, but ye are washed, ye are sanctified. When men repent and so give evidence of reconciliation they are no longer the persons they were; but so long as they continue such, they have no friendship with God. Ellicott states the same edge differently: the unworthy Christian does have an inheritance in the kingdom, to his own awful responsibility, but in the spiritual sense he is one who has not, and from whom what he has will be taken. Robertson raises a smaller question about the title. Paul's single article before Christ and God might be read as an assertion of Christ's deity, though he will not press the rule here, since the word for God is often definite without the article, like a proper name — adding only that Paul taught the deity of Christ elsewhere and may be doing it here. Gill notes the variant that turns the opening clause into an imperative, know ye this.

Who the deceivers with vain words were is disputed. Ellicott and Robertson both look to an early Antinomian Gnosticism, which held that what is done in the body, evil only by the inevitable gravitation of matter, cannot touch the soul; Ellicott finds the same warning in the Ephesian John's insistence that he who does righteousness is righteous. Clarke looks instead at the city, and documents it. He cites Athenaeus that the Ephesians were given to luxury, that Aspasia filled Greece with prostitutes, and that Ephesus had dedicated temples to Venus under that title; and he quotes the notorious sentence from Demosthenes dividing women into three classes, for pleasure, for daily use, and for legitimate children. The greatest lawgivers and wisest philosophers, he observes, upheld the system by authority and example alike — and asks whether it is not their teaching that Paul means by vain words. Barnes takes a middle line, supposing plausible arguments from friends still moving in those circles, and noting that not a few philosophers defended such practices and practised them too. Calvin hears the excuses themselves: this is a trivial fault, God views fornication lightly, under grace he is not so cruel, the frailty of nature excuses us. Wesley says only that the heathen esteemed them innocent.
8:
Paul does not say they walked in darkness but that they were darkness, and Ellicott makes the difference the point. The outward element is said to pervade the inner nature, so that Christ is the true Light and his servants are secondary lights kindled from his rays, reflecting rather than originating, and becoming light only in the Lord. The converse is worse than the ordinary phrase would allow: those who are darkness are new sources of it, and as there is a natural delight in giving light, so the reprobate state is marked by a horrible pleasure in spreading the cloud of delusion by which God is hidden from men. Calvin uses the same term for the whole nature of man before regeneration, on the ground that where the brightness of God does not shine there is nothing but fearful darkness, and that out of Christ everything lies under the dominion of the prince of darkness. Gill adds the local colour, that the Jews were accustomed to call the Gentiles darkness itself.

The next verse turns on a textual variant, and every voice in the catena notices it. Where the received text reads the fruit of the Spirit, Clarke reports the leading uncials and the Syriac, Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Itala reading the fruit of the light, and says most critics take it for the true reading, since the Spirit is not mentioned anywhere in the context. Gill notes the same reading in the Alexandrian copy and observes that it agrees with the words just before. Robertson reports it flatly, that the late manuscripts have Spirit where the earlier have light, and enjoys the doubled metaphor of fruit and light together. Calvin professes to wonder how the word Spirit crept into so many Greek copies, judging the other reading more consistent — while adding, characteristically, that Paul's meaning is not affected either way. Wesley simply adopts the better reading and sets the fruit of the light against the unfruitful works of darkness.

Ellicott presses the metaphor further than the others: light has fruits and darkness has none, which is not merely a figure but literally so, since light is the condition of the vegetative life that grows and bears while darkness destroys fruit-bearing if not life itself. On the three qualities named he takes goodness for love in practical benevolence, and righteousness and truth as parts of the single principle of being true. Clarke orders them as a sequence — goodness in the principle and disposition, righteousness in the exercise of that goodness through the whole conduct of life, and truth as the director of both toward God's glory and the good of mankind. Barnes reduces the first to a test: he who is not good is not a Christian. On the participle that follows, Barnes reports Rosenmüller taking it for an imperative and Chandler for a statement that they discerned and approved what pleased God, while Ellicott defines proving as trying each case by the full light of God, partly a work of thought and partly of practical experience. Gill insists the trial be made by the Scriptures and not by human reason, which is corrupt and fallible, and in some things outreached by revelation.
11:
Ellicott sharpens what the prohibition asks. To have no fellowship is not merely to refuse to take part, which could be assumed, but to keep no terms with such works — no sympathy, no indulgence, no excuse; and it is by weak or cowardly indulgence, he adds, rather than by any love of evil, that sin is generally suffered to prevail. Gill draws the necessary limit from the wording, noticing that Paul forbids fellowship with the works and not with the workers: ordinary civil dealing with such men is not prohibited, and is warranted by the greatest examples, especially where there is any prospect of doing good to them. Clarke reads the phrase against the local cults, taking the works of darkness for the mysteries celebrated at night in caves and dark recesses, unfruitful because of no use to mankind and secret on pain of death — whence, he notes, they were called unspeakable — and adds the magic and incantations to which Ephesus was notoriously given. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the clause for a different purpose, warning catechumens against teachers who held that Christ was assembled out of contributions from twenty-nine aeons: shun their impiety, he says, and do not even greet such a man.

What "reprove" governs is disputed, and the answer changes the sense. Calvin reports that most expositors supply the doers of the works as the object and take the verb for wholesome correction, but judges that harsh, preferring to supply the works themselves and to render it as bringing them to the light so that their evil nature is shown — a reading he says the following verse requires. Robertson defines it in the same key, to convict by turning the light on the darkness. Clarke keeps the personal object and lets the verb carry its whole range: bear a testimony against them, convince them that they are wrong, confute them in their vain reasons, reprove them for vices that are flagrant while they pretend to superior illumination. Barnes takes the reproving to be done chiefly without words, by a life, a conversation and an influence which stand as a standing rebuke of a sinful world. Calvin adds why the duty is neglected: where an offence against God is manifest, every man is eager to clear himself of any share in the guilt, but very few guard against connivance, and nearly all practise some kind of dissimulation.

The clause about shame in speaking draws the sharpest modern application in the chapter. Barnes turns it on the reforming zeal of his own day and asks whether, if the apostle would not let them so much as name these things, it is wise for ministers to portray them from the pulpit or for the friends of moral reform to describe them to the world; the naming produces improper associations, the description raises polluting images, and the exhibition of pictures defiles even when it condemns. Ellicott says the same more briefly — sin may be plainly indicated and most effectively branded without polluting the tongue by describing what it actually does — and observes that the need of the caution is obvious in some satires against vice and some manuals of self-examination. Clarke supplies what Paul would not, naming the Bacchanalian rites that the Roman senate itself banished from Italy. Against all this Robertson enters one qualification: sometimes a man must speak out and turn on the light, even though doing so is disgraceful. Wesley closes the argument on the light itself, that nothing but light, and light from heaven, can make anything manifest at all.
14:
Where the quotation comes from is the standing puzzle of the chapter, and everyone works at it. Barnes reports that it is agreed on all hands not to be found in so many words in the older Scriptures, and disposes of the two usual candidates. The first, promising the dust to awake and sing, is not a quotation at all and resembles this only in the word awake, while its subject is entirely different. The second, bidding Zion arise and shine because her light is come, is addressed to the church in her triumph, whereas this is addressed to individuals in their sin; in design the two have no resemblance whatever. He then lists the conjectures of a lost source: Epiphanius took it for a prophecy of Elijah, Syncellus and Euthalius for a writing of Jeremiah, Hippolytus for some prophet now unknown, Jerome for an apocryphal book. Ellicott reaches the same dead end by another route, judging the nearest parallel certainly very far off and concluding that we are driven to say the words are not Scripture — yet their very form shows they came from something well known. Gill canvasses the same list and adds the suggestion that it was a saying of Christ still fresh in memory.

Two solutions remain, and the catena is split between them. Ellicott and Clarke both propose a Christian hymn. Clarke notes that hymns and spiritual songs are named a few verses later, prints the three Greek lines as they would have stood, and credits the suggestion to earlier scholars; Ellicott finds a rhythmical character in the original, rough but by no means indistinct, and connects the guess with the growth of set formulas in the later letters, where memory did the work that writing does for us. Robertson agrees that the last line raises the possibility of an early Christian hymn, while still calling the whole a free adaptation of Isaiah. Clarke, however, offers a second and quite different reading, taking the verb impersonally and referring it to the light — that is, to the gospel named just before — so that what follows is not a citation at all but the standing voice of the gospel everywhere. Calvin arrives independently at almost the same place. Rather than hunt a passage nowhere to be found, he takes Christ to be speaking through his ministers, since this is the ordinary message delivered every day by preachers, whose whole object is to raise the dead to life. Wesley supplies the subject as God, speaking in the general tenor of his word.

On the substance Clarke presses both figures. A sleeping man neither knows nor does anything that can be called good, and the heathen accordingly had no proper notion of vice and virtue nor any true idea of God; a dead man performs no function of life, and the unconverted were incapable of anything worthy of life. Yet the sleeper may be woken by a voice, and their animal life and reason being whole in them, the gospel had something to call to. Calvin guards the last clause against a misreading it invites. It does not mean that Christ's light begins to shine on us after we have risen, as if our performance came before his grace; the sense is that when Christ enlightens us we rise from death to life at that moment. Wesley glosses the three terms in order — asleep in ignorance of God and of oneself, dead in sin, and given light in knowledge, holiness and happiness. Robertson notes that the verb for shining is a rare form found in Job rather than the common one, and Calvin dismisses a competing reading of it as an evident blunder, observing that Chrysostom had already noticed the variation and decided for the received form.
15:
"Circumspectly" is challenged by the two who look hardest at the Greek. Clarke grants that the English word, from the Latin, means looking round on all hands and being wary of danger, but says the original signifies correctly, accurately, consistently — walk by the rule God has given, in little things as in great, so that no enemy can say you are holy in profession and irregular in life. Ellicott agrees and presses the point: the word is elsewhere used of intellectual accuracy and only here and in one other place of moral strictness, so the idea is not of looking about for dangers but of finding the clear line of right and keeping to it exactly, in order not to run uncertainly. Barnes and Gill keep the traditional sense, Barnes taking it as anxious care against the temptations around them and Gill as walking with the eyes about one, with diligence and caution to the uttermost of one's strength. Robertson contributes a small textual point, that the best manuscripts put the adverb before the interrogative, so that the sentence reads see carefully how ye walk rather than see how carefully ye walk.

Chrysostom supplies a setting the later commentators do not. These readers were sheep among wolves and commanded not to defend themselves; whole cities were at war with them, and the war had made its way into their houses, dividing father against son and mother against daughter. Lest they should think the gospel was needlessly making quarrels, Paul tells them to look carefully how they walk — meaning, give no handle for hatred on any score except the gospel message itself, and let that be the only ground of it. Clarke fastens instead on the pair of words that follows, noting that the heathen liked to be called wise, that Pythagoras corrected the vanity by calling himself only a lover of wisdom — whence philosopher, a word now used far more proudly than he intended — and that Paul takes the title for the Christian and leaves the Gentile philosopher the name of fool. Ellicott defines the wisdom in question as the practical knowledge of the true end and purpose of life, so that a man may have great intellectual and spiritual gifts and still be unwise. Calvin adds the motive: men on whom the Sun of righteousness has risen stand as in a crowded theatre, under the eye of God and of angels.

On redeeming the time, Ellicott would rather say the opportunity, and shows from the Aramaic of Daniel — where the phrase is used in a bad sense of gaining time to escape a difficulty — that the verb means buying up for oneself rather than ransoming. Applied to opportunity it implies making a sacrifice for it, seizing it quickly, and using it to the utmost, whether by silence or speech, by facing danger or avoiding it; the lesson, he says, is the one drawn in the parable of the unjust steward, that the children of light should show the shrewdness of the buyers and sellers of the world. Calvin asks what the price of the redemption is and answers that it is withdrawal from the endless allurements that lead men astray, and the abandoning of every hindrance. Barnes measures the supply against the demand: a man who has a soul to save need never have an idle moment, and God has given exactly enough time for the purposes he designs and no more. Wesley speaks of buying every possible moment out of the hands of sloth and ease. Henry turns the excuse round — people are very apt to complain of bad times, and it were well if that stirred them more to redeem the time.
18:
Three of them hear the Bacchic festivals behind the prohibition, and read the verse as a contrast between two inspirations. Barnes recalls that men and women counted it an acceptable act of worship to become intoxicated and to run through streets and vineyards with wild songs, and cites Plato's remark that while those ceremonies lasted it was hard to find a sober man in all Attica; against this Paul sets psalms and hymns, so that Christian worship should stand out against the wild habits of the heathen. Clarke pushes the etymology of the verb for getting drunk back to the sacrifice after which the drinking followed, and notes that Plato, who condemned drunkenness generally, allowed it at the solemnities of the god who invented wine. His sharpest point is about the priests, who professed to be filled with the influence of the god they served and delivered their oracles in that condition — which is exactly what Paul tells the Ephesians not to resemble. Ellicott states the same contrast analytically: drunkenness is not, like gluttony, primarily an appetite gratified, but a reckless pursuit of excitement at any cost, celebrated by writers like Horace as a quickener of wit and confused in the Dionysiac frenzy with divine inspiration itself.

The word rendered "excess" is stronger than the English suggests. Calvin reports that it is built from a negative and the verb to save, so that it pictures a man past saving, and notes it is the adverb used of the prodigal's living in the far country; from which he concludes that drunkards throw off every restraint of modesty quickly, since where wine reigns profligacy follows of course. Robertson observes that the imperative is present and passive, forbidding the habit and requiring anyone already in it to stop. Gill sets the boundaries of the prohibition with care: wine is named only because it was the common drink of those countries and the rule covers any strong liquor; drinking for necessary use, and for honest delight and lawful pleasure, is not forbidden; and it is a habit rather than a single act that makes a drunkard, since a man may be overtaken through ignorance of the liquor's strength. He adds that those who are not drunkards themselves but are the means of it in others are criminal too. Wesley states the substitution simply, that the Spirit gives a nobler pleasure than wine can. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the whole clause among his proofs that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives and speaks.

What the three kinds of song are divides them along a familiar line. Gill argues that all three names denote the one Book of Psalms — hymns being only another title for it, since the running head might as well be the Book of Hymns, the psalm sung after the supper is called a hymn, and Philo and Josephus call the psalms hymns and songs alike. Clarke distinguishes them sharply: psalms are probably David's, hymns are extemporaneous effusions uttered under the influence of the Spirit, and odes are premeditated and regular poetic compositions, all of them spiritual in tendency. Ellicott separates them by their music rather than their authorship, the psalm being accompanied and almost certainly the old psalter, the hymn purely vocal and probably naming the new utterances of the Christian church, the spiritual song harder to place; he cites Pliny's description of Christians singing a hymn among themselves by turns. Wesley draws the boldest inference from the silence — that since no inspired songs were given for the Christian dispensation as they had been for the Jewish, the larger effusion of the Spirit was meant to supply the lack. Clarke ends where the verse does, calling it a shocking profanation to draw near with the lips while the heart is far off.
20:
"For all things" may not mean things at all. Barnes reports Barrow's view that the phrase should be rendered for all persons, so that Christians are bound to give thanks for the mercies bestowed on the human race, and he finds the same sense in the Prayer Book's thanks for God's loving-kindness to us and to all men and in the apostolic charge that thanksgiving be made for all men. Ellicott keeps the ordinary rendering and describes the temper it asks for: since thanksgiving is for what God has given and prayer for what we still need, the two must go together in our imperfect condition, and a thankfulness that prevails alike in joy and sorrow, undisturbed even by a penitent sense of sin, becomes the inner music of a Christian life. He marks it also as the fundamental and invariable element of public worship, clothing itself naturally in every variety of music. Gill lists what falls under it, temporal mercies and spiritual alike, and insists on the adverb — at all times, in adversity, desertion, temptation and persecution as well as in prosperity. Wesley gives the reason in five words, that all things work together for good.

The clause about mutual submission is read as the hinge of everything that follows. Barnes takes it as the general principle to be applied in turn to wives, children and servants, and states its point polemically: Christianity does not break up the relations of life or produce disorder and insubordination but confirms every proper authority and makes every just yoke lighter — infidelity is always disorganising, and Christianity never. Ellicott suspects a specific occasion for the emphasis, since the New Testament insists so often on subjection to civil, domestic and church authority alike, and thinks this indicates a tendency, in the first exuberance of Christian liberty, to disregard the wholesome restraints and conventions of outward life. Henry describes the temper rather than the structure: a mutual condescension in which men bear one another's burdens instead of advancing themselves above others or giving laws to one another, of which Paul himself was the example in becoming all things to all men. Calvin refuses to exempt anyone, not even kings and governors, whose authority exists for the service of the community; and knowing that nothing is more irksome to human nature than mutual subjection, he points to the fear named in the clause as the only thing that can subdue our fierceness. Robertson notes the military figure in the verb, of falling into line under another.

The last two words carry a variant, and the two who notice it come out on opposite sides. Clarke reports that where the received text reads the fear of God, the leading uncials and most other manuscripts, with the Syriac, Coptic, Sahidic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate and Itala, together with Basil and Chrysostom, read the fear of Christ; and he adds that neither reading makes any difference to the sense. Calvin knows the same evidence and draws the opposite conclusion, suspecting that the change was introduced by someone who found the received phrase, though by far the most appropriate, a little harsh to the ear — while granting that it does not much affect the meaning whether the fear is taken passively, as submission because we fear Christ, or actively, as the temper that ought to govern godly minds under his reign. Ellicott observes that the clause faces both ways: grammatically it belongs with the verses before it, and in sense it opens the section on the threefold submission of wives, children and slaves that occupies the rest of the letter's practical part. Clarke adds the small practical rider that no man should be so tenacious of his own opinion in matters indifferent as to disturb the peace of the church.
22:
Chrysostom opens the section by praising the bond rather than the ordinance. A wise man, he recalls, set a wife agreeing with her husband among the blessings, and elsewhere counted it a blessing that a woman should live in harmony with her husband; and God made special provision for the union from the beginning, speaking of the two as one when he made them male and female. No relationship between man and man, he insists, is as close as that between man and wife where they are joined as they should be — which is why the mourner in the old story, wanting a word for surpassing love, named neither father nor mother nor child nor brother nor friend, but said that the love was wonderful, passing the love of women. He ends with a formulation the later commentators never match: this love is more despotic than any despotism, since other affections may be strong, but this one is not only strong but unfading. Gill states the plain content of the duty in the same register — thinking well of a husband, speaking respectfully of him, imitating what is good in him and bearing with what is not, and abiding with him in adversity as in prosperity.

Every one of them limits the command, and some limit it sharply. Wesley makes the exception first — unless where God forbids — and then adds a structural observation the others miss, that throughout this section the inferior party is named before the superior, because the general proposition is about submission and inferiors must do their duty whatever their superiors do. Clarke states the limit at length. It is every lawful thing that is meant, and nothing criminal; a husband may be profligate and wish his wife to be so too, or an enemy of religion using his authority to keep her from the means of grace, and in none of these things is she to obey him. He is equally blunt about the other side, that the husband is not to be a tyrant nor the wife the governor, and quotes Quarles's rhyme about the household with a silent cock and a crowing hen. Barnes holds that Christianity elevated the wife without abolishing subordination, and warns the husband to be as cautious about invading her prerogative as she about invading his. Gill narrows the scope: the subjection is to her husband only, and not to any other man, nor to her children, nor to those in her house.

The comparison with Christ carries a qualification that Robertson calls a tremendous difference, hastily added: he is himself the saviour of the body. Ellicott traces what follows from it by setting the verse beside the parallel in the earlier letter, where headship is simple lordship in a chain running from woman to man to Christ to God. Here the headship of Christ over the whole church takes the place of his headship over the individual, and from that comes the further idea of a spiritual unity which requires self-sacrifice in the head as much as obedience to him — so that the third clause of the earlier chain has nothing to correspond to it. Barnes turns the difference into the husband's charge: as Christ gave himself to save his body, so the husband is to be his wife's natural protector, anticipating her wants and comforting her in trial. Clarke says the same in fewer words, that authority is to be exercised by protecting and providing. Calvin refers the qualifying pronoun to Christ and reasons from it that nothing yields a wife more advantage than subjection, so that to refuse the means of her safety is to choose destruction. Henry sums the whole relation up as unity and love, in which failures on both sides alter nothing.
25:
Robertson calls the comparison the wonderful new point, absent from the parallel letter, which lifts the whole discussion to its highest plane. Clarke draws the consequence for authority: the husband's rule over his wife is founded on his love to her, and that love must be such as would lead him to risk his life for her — more, therefore, than protection and support, since as Christ gave himself to save the church, a husband should labour by every means to promote his wife's salvation. He adds a domestic reason often left unsaid, that since the care of the family falls on her and the children owe the forming of their manners chiefly to their mother, she needs all the assistance her husband can give. Ellicott makes the same point as a condition: only so far as a husband shows the like love, in perfect sympathy, in chivalrous forbearance, in abhorrence of tyranny and in willingness to sacrifice himself, has he any right to claim lordship at all. Barnes offers the rule in its simplest form, that a husband is in no danger of loving his wife too much provided she is not loved more than God. Ellicott and Robertson both mark where the likeness stops: in the atoning character of the sacrifice, none can approach him.

"The washing of water" is read by nearly all of them as baptism, and the differences lie in what is granted to it. Ellicott renders the clause as cleansing in the laver of the water in the Word, calls the reference to baptism unquestionable, and takes the added phrase of the word as audibly spoken — the question of faith, the answer of a good conscience, and the baptismal formula itself. Robertson weighs whether the noun means the bath or the bathing, and inclines to the bath, but denies that Paul means the cleansing took place in it except symbolically. Calvin states the guard most fully. When Paul says we are washed by baptism his meaning is that God employs it to declare to us that we are washed, and at the same time performs what it represents; but we must beware of ascribing to the sign or to the minister what belongs to God alone, lest, as has often happened, a sacrament be turned into an idol. Wesley makes the same reservation in a clause — in baptism, if with the outward and visible sign we receive the inward and spiritual grace. Gill takes a different road altogether, referring the cleansing less to inward sanctification than to justification by the blood and righteousness of Christ.

The presentation is a wedding scene, and Clarke traces it to the royal bride brought to the king in raiment of needlework, with the bridal purifications of Esther behind the cleansing — six months with oil of myrrh and six with sweet odours. He reads the two defects precisely: no blemish on the face and no stain on the garment, and no wrinkle, which is the mark of decay rather than of dirt. Barnes suggests that prepare would render the verb better than present, and cites Tindale's making it unto himself. Calvin points out what the verse cannot be made to prove: the Pelagians used it for the perfection of righteousness in this life, and Augustine answered them; the design of the washing is that we should not return to our pollution but keep the purity once received. Cyril of Jerusalem, preaching to candidates for baptism, presses the timing with unusual care. He does not mean, he tells them, that they should be without spot or wrinkle before receiving the grace — how could that be, when it is for the remission of sins that they have been called? — but that when the grace is about to be given, their conscience, being found uncondemned, may concur with it.
28:
Calvin puts the argument as a syllogism drawn from nature. Every man by his very nature loves himself; no man can love himself without loving his wife, since marriage was appointed on the condition that the two should be one; therefore the man who does not love his wife is a monster. Gill notes that the language was proverbial among Paul's countrymen, whose maxim was that a man's wife is as his own body and who taught that he should honour her more than his body and love her as his body. Ellicott corrects a small misreading with large consequences: the "so" that opens the verse looks back to the love of Christ just described, not forward to the comparison that follows, and it is from that pattern that everything after it grows — Christ loving the church as his body, so that the earlier idea of headship gives way to an absolute identification of the husband with his wife. Robertson breaks off to defend the apostle, asking how anyone can say that Paul's treatment of marriage elsewhere is degrading, after reading what he judges the noblest picture of marriage ever drawn.

The two verbs are read as feeding and clothing. Barnes takes the first to mean bringing up, as one brings up children, and the second to mean warming, so that between them they cover food and raiment; he supports the premise from the classics, citing Curtius that we do not hate what belongs to our own bodies and Seneca's confession that a love of our own body is implanted in us. Robertson notes that the word for cherishing is rare enough to be traceable to a marriage contract in a papyrus, and that it means first to warm and then to foster with tender care. Wesley reduces the pair to feeding and clothing. Ellicott adds the point that gives the comparison its edge — a husband is to care for his wife not simply as a self but as a weaker self, for whom he is bound to think and act — and observes that the figure itself assumes the Christian estimate of the body as part of the true self and a temple of God, which is flatly incompatible with the Gnostic view of matter as the source of evil that was beginning to trouble the Asian churches.

The closing clause about flesh and bones divides them three ways. Robertson denies that the words belong in the text at all, noting that the received reading is supported by later manuscripts and the Syriac but is wanting in the leading uncials, and pronouncing it certainly not genuine. Gill and Barnes accept the words but refuse them any literal force. Gill argues that the reference cannot be to Christ's natural body, which would make his humanity monstrous, since our flesh and bones come from the first Adam and are corrupt; Paul is speaking of the saints not as men but as Christians, and therefore of the mystical body. Barnes traces the phrase to Adam's words about Eve and warns against language implying a miraculous union: it is not physical but a union of attachment, of feeling, of love. Calvin will not have it weakened. This is no exaggeration but the simple truth, he says, and Paul means something higher than that Christ merely shares our nature. Clarke keeps to the middle ground, that Christ partook of our nature as we partook of Adam's, and that members of the church are united to him by one Spirit as members are to a body.
31:
What "for this cause" refers back to decides how mystical the verse is allowed to be. Ellicott thinks it far simpler to treat the clause about flesh and bones as parenthetical and to look back two verses, so that the sense is: because a man's wife is as his own body, therefore shall a man leave his father and mother. Connecting it instead with the words immediately before is possible, he grants, but somewhat too mystical even for this passage. Robertson goes further and calls it absurd to make the "man" of the quotation mean Christ, as some commentators do. Ellicott also draws the distinction the quotation turns on: the tie of parentage belongs to the natural relations we are born into and do not make, while marriage is the most sacred of the ties we make for ourselves. Clarke supplies the strongest image in the chapter for what the joining means. The verb is to be glued or cemented, and as a well-glued board will sooner break in the solid wood than at the joint, so death alone can part husband and wife. Wesley gives the reason in five words — because of this intimate union — and Gill notes that the verse has always been urged against polygamy.

"A great mystery" became a battleground because of a Latin word. Barnes reports that the Vulgate renders it a great sacrament, and says this is the only proof ever adduced that marriage is one; but the Greek conveys no such idea, meaning something concealed and hitherto unknown, into which a man must be initiated — not something unintelligible once disclosed. Clarke says the same and adds that on the evidence of that version the Church of Rome made matrimony a sacrament, which is no meaning of the original; a mystery here is a natural thing by which something spiritual is signified. Ellicott, who also traces the sacramental usage to the Latin, extends the word to the type as well as the antitype: the indissoluble sacredness of marriage is itself a secret of God's law fully revealed only in Christ, since heathen and to some degree Jewish thought held marriage a contract far less sacred than the tie of blood — and wherever Christian principle is renounced, he observes, that older idea returns. Calvin makes no attempt to define it. He is overwhelmed by the depth of the thing, and is not ashamed to join Paul in confessing at once his ignorance and his admiration.

The chapter ends by coming back to earth, which Ellicott notes is characteristic of the apostle after high and mysterious teaching. Robertson describes the grammar of the return as an unusual idiom, the verb agreeing with each individually rather than with the plural, and the wife's clause standing without any governing verb at all, an elliptical imperative; the word rendered reverence, he adds, means fear in the sense of reverence. Barnes takes it the same way, as honour and respect rather than dread, and explains it by the ordering of the household rather than by any comparison of worth. A note carried in Calvin's column, credited to Eadie, gives the neatest account of why the two commands are not symmetrical: what is instinctive on either side is not enjoined, but what is needed to direct and hallow that instinct is. The woman loves already, and is therefore told to honour and obey, so that her fondness may know its sphere; the man already feels that his place is to govern, and is therefore told to love, so that he may learn what the substance of his government should be. Gill observes only that Paul now recapitulates, and would have every married person take the directions to himself.
